1.pericope_label: No date given: the day of the Lord comes as a thief
debates: What day is meant: Clarke reads the times and seasons and the sudden destruction chiefly of the fall of Jerusalem in the Roman war, while Gill, Henry, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin take the whole of the second advent

How much the readers already knew: Ellicott and Robertson hold that what they knew accurately was their own ignorance, an oxymoron, while Barnes and Calvin take it that they knew the manner of the coming, its suddenness, with certainty
outliers: Chrysostom's diagnosis of the question as the restlessness of an unsettled and unoccupied mind, illustrated from children teasing their nurses and from the apostles asking the same thing twice
Calvin's inference that the hiding of the day is itself the purpose, so that being kept in suspense we might be as it were upon watch
Barnes's argument that destruction here means the pulling down of what a thing is rather than annihilation, and that it cannot be reconciled with universal salvation

4.pericope_label: Children of the day: not asleep, not drunken
debates: Whether the text reads as a thief or as thieves: Ellicott reports that two of the best manuscripts, the Coptic, Lachmann and Lightfoot support the plural, but defends the received singular as better attested and better suited to the context, and Robertson notes the same witnesses

What the darkness stands for: Ellicott insists the chief thought is torpor and inattention rather than ignorance or sin, while Gill takes it for the whole state of unregeneracy and Clarke for the condition of those judged in the night
outliers: Clarke's citation of the Midrash on the Psalms, that God will judge the Gentiles by night while they sleep in their transgressions but the Israelites by day while they study the law, which he thinks underlies five verses together

Ellicott's note that children of light is a Hebrew idiom of natural affinity, so that the day can never come to such men as a startling apparition, and his remark that the shift from ye to we is a courtesy

Ellicott's report from Cyprian that Christians were known from other men because their breath smelt of wine in the early morning, from attending the Sacrament at an hour when no heathen would have touched it
themes: the judgment of Jew and Gentile

8.pericope_label: The armour, the appointment, and the comfort drawn from both
debates: Who is appointed to wrath: Gill takes it of vessels of wrath ordained of old to condemnation, Clarke restricts it to the Jewish nation and dates the appointment from their final rejection of the gospel, denying that it means eternal damnation, and Wesley refers it to the obstinately impenitent

Whether the salvation is acquired or received: Ellicott presses the word to mean earning by one's own efforts and says God does not predestinate men to salvation without laborious acquisition on their part, while Calvin denies that we procure salvation and says we obtain what Christ acquired

Whether the armour should be expounded piece by piece: Calvin and Ellicott both say no, Calvin because Paul differs from himself in Ephesians and Ellicott because the assignments look far-fetched, while Clarke assigns a function to each
outliers: Ellicott's remark that we ourselves are the only persons who can defeat God's predestinations
Barnes's illustration from the ancients consulting the flight of birds and the entrails of animals for assurance that the gods would give the victory, set against the unerring assurance of the word
Calvin's soldier's argument, that men intemperate in other situations refrain from every bodily delight when the enemy is near, so believers should be at least as vigilant as soldiers

12.pericope_label: Knowing those who labour, and the discipline of the flock
debates: Who is charged to warn the unruly: Barnes says the exhortation is evidently to the whole church and not to the ministers only, while Ellicott holds that the writers turn to the presbytery and set out their duty in administering discipline, and says the same of the charge not to render evil for evil
Whether the three descriptions mark different orders of ministers: Barnes and Robertson both deny it and take them for different functions of the same leaders
outliers: Chrysostom's comparison of the priest with the physician and the father, both of whom may give pain and keep their standing, whereas whoever the priest reproves is sure to become an enemy, and grieves at the public disgrace rather than at the loss of the prayers

Calvin's test drawn from the titles themselves, that labour excludes all idle bellies from the number of pastors and instruction excludes any who glory in the name without teaching, with the inference that judgment is committed to the Church to distinguish true pastors
Wesley's outburst against the man who undertakes the whole work without gifts or graces for any part of it and sells his own soul and the souls of the flock for pay
Ellicott's observation that abstinence from revenge was practically a new thought among Greeks, whose feuds were frequent and undying

16.pericope_label: Rejoice, pray, give thanks, and do not quench the Spirit
debates: What is quenched: Gill takes the graces of the Spirit, which may be damped but not lost, Robertson takes the special gifts, Clarke expressly denies that the miraculous gifts can be meant because the direction here is general, and Ellicott warns against taking the word of the Person at all

Whether the clause about the will of God enforces a duty or offers encouragement: Ellicott insists it is the latter, that God has no wish to give cause for sorrow, while Barnes and Clarke read it as the thing God requires
outliers: Barnes recalling that Chrysostom, driven into exile and dying far from the capital, kept repeating his motto, glory to God for all things
Wesley calling the three commands together Christian perfection, beyond which we cannot go and short of which we need not stop
Chrysostom's working of the lamp into a rule for the tongue, that the mouth is the door and an open one adds force to the wind of an insult, whereas shutting it leaves no draught and spends the blast
Clarke's note that four manuscripts of good note add the words in the Lord to the command to rejoice

20.pericope_label: Prophesying, proving, and what to hold fast
debates: What the last clause forbids: Gill, Barnes and Clarke read it of the appearance of evil, Ellicott says that translation cannot stand and renders every evil kind, Robertson supports kind from the papyri, and Calvin rejects both and applies it to doctrine merely suspected of falsity

Why prophecy was despised at Thessalonica: Barnes suspects the showier gift of tongues was preferred, while Ellicott rejects that view for want of evidence and traces it to a despondency that damped all ardour alike
What prophesying is: Calvin, Wesley, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all take it of preaching or interpretation, while Gill extends it to the written prophecies of both Testaments
outliers: Barnes's claim that Christianity is more than any other religion the friend of free inquiry, requiring no man to accept what synods and councils have decreed and no opinion whatever its antiquity until he is convinced it is true

Calvin's inference that the spirit of discrimination must be conferred on believers, since otherwise the command to prove all things would have been given in vain, and his declaration that heaven and earth may be commingled rather than that prophecy should cease
Calvin's polemic against those who despise the ministry of man and Scripture itself in order to attain the Spirit, and set forth as secret revelations whatever is breathed into their ears

23.pericope_label: Sanctified whole: the closing prayer, greetings and adjuration
debates: Whether man is of three parts: Ellicott and Clarke take the division strictly, Calvin accepts it but assigns reason to the spirit and will and affections to the soul, Robertson says it is not necessarily trichotomy as against dichotomy, and Wesley denies it outright on the ground that the soul is either matter, and so part of the body, or not matter, and so coincides with the spirit

Whether entire sanctification is attainable in this life: Clarke says it is not to take place in, at, or after death, while Barnes warns that a prayer for perfect sanctification is no proof that it is attained here and Henry holds that the best are sanctified only in part
outliers: Ellicott dissenting on the placing of the soul from the bishop whose name the commentary he writes in bears

Barnes's argument that the animal nature must be included in the prayer, since for a lion to rage or the ostrich to leave her eggs involves no guilt, they being unaccountable, whereas the same temper in a man does
Calvin's charge that those who forbid the people to read the writings of Paul are more refractory than devils themselves, since they are unmoved by so strict an adjuration

Ellicott's report that one critic read the adjuration as the mark of a forger seeking authority for his work, answered by another who found in the constant public recitation a guarantee of the letter's integrity
